# A Drama Of Three

It was a regular dramatic performance every first of the month in the little cottage of the old General and Madame B----.

It began with the waking up of the General by his wife, standing at the bedside with a cup of black coffee.

"Hé! Ah! Oh, Honorine! Yes; the first of the month, and affairs--affairs to be transacted."

On those mornings when affairs were to be transacted there was not much leisure for the household; and it was Honorine who constituted the household. Not the old dressing-gown and slippers, the old, old trousers, and the antediluvian neck-foulard of other days! Far from it. It was a case of warm water (with even a fling of cologne in it), of the trimming of beard and mustache by Honorine, and the black broadcloth suit, and the brown satin stock, and that _je ne sais quoi de dégagé_ which no one could possess or assume like the old General. Whether he possessed or assumed it is an uncertainty which hung over the fine manners of all the gentlemen of his day, who were kept through their youth in Paris to cultivate _bon ton_ and an education.

It was also something of a gala-day for Madame la Générale too, as it must be a gala-day for all old wives to see their husbands pranked in the manners and graces that had conquered their maidenhood, and exhaling once more that ambrosial fragrance which once so well incensed their compelling presence.

Ah, to the end a woman loves to celebrate her conquest! It is the last touch of misfortune with her to lose in the old, the ugly, and the commonplace her youthful lord and master. If one could look under the gray hairs and wrinkles with which time thatches old women, one would be surprised to see the flutterings, the quiverings, the thrills, the emotions, the coals of the heart-fires which death alone extinguishes, when he commands the tenant to vacate.

Honorine's hands chilled with the ice of sixteen as she approached scissors to the white mustache and beard. When her finger-tips brushed those lips, still well formed and roseate, she felt it, strange to say, on her lips. When she asperged the warm water with cologne,--it was her secret delight and greatest effort of economy to buy this cologne,--she always had one little moment of what she called faintness--that faintness which had veiled her eyes, and chained her hands, and stilled her throbbing bosom, when as a bride she came from the church with him. It was then she noticed the faint fragrance of the cologne bath. Her lips would open as they did then, and she would stand for a moment and think thoughts to which, it must be confessed, she looked forward from month to month. What a man he had been! In truth he belonged to a period that would accept nothing less from Nature than physical beauty; and Nature is ever subservient to the period. If it is to-day all small men, and to-morrow gnomes and dwarfs, we may know that the period is demanding them from Nature.

When the General had completed--let it be called no less than the ceremony of--his toilet, he took his chocolate and his _pain de Paris_. Honorine could not imagine him breakfasting on anything but _pain de Paris._ Then he sat himself in his large arm-chair before his escritoire, and began transacting his affairs with the usual--

"But where is that idiot, that dolt, that sluggard, that snail, with my mail?" Honorine, busy in the breakfast-room:

"In a moment, husband. In a moment."

"But he should be here now. It is the first of the month, it is nine o'clock, I am ready; he should be here."

"It is not yet nine o'clock, husband."

"Not yet nine! Not yet nine! Am I not up? Am I not dressed? Have I not breakfasted before nine?"

"That is so, husband. That is so." Honorine's voice, prompt in cheerful acquiescence, came from the next room, where she was washing his cup, saucer, and spoon.

"It is getting worse and worse every day. I tell you, Honorine, Pompey must be discharged. He is worthless. He is trifling. Discharge him! Discharge him! Do not have him about! Chase him out of the yard! Chase him as soon as he makes his appearance! Do you hear, Honorine?"

"You must have a little patience, husband."

It was perhaps the only reproach one could make to Madame Honorine, that she never learned by experience.

"Patience! Patience! Patience is the invention of dullards and sluggards. In a well-regulated world there should be no need of such a thing as patience. Patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace. Wherever patience is found police investigation should be made as for smallpox. Patience! Patience! I never heard the word--I assure you, I never heard the word in Paris. What do you think would be said there to the messenger who craved patience of you? Oh, they know too well in Paris--a rataplan from the walking-stick on his back, that would be the answer; and a, 'My good fellow, we are not hiring professors of patience, but legs.'"

"But, husband, you must remember we do not hire Pompey. He only does it to oblige us, out of his kindness."

"Oblige us! Oblige me! Kindness! A negro oblige me! Kind to me! That is it; that is it. That is the way to talk under the new régime. It is favor, and oblige, and education, and monsieur, and madame, now. What child's play to call this a country--a government! I would not be surprised"--jumping to his next position on this ever-recurring first of the month theme--"I would not be surprised if Pompey has failed to find the letter in the box. How do I know that the mail has not been tampered with? From day to day I expect to hear it. What is to prevent? Who is to interpose? The honesty of the officials? Honesty of the officials--that is good! What a farce--honesty of officials! That is evidently what has happened. The thought has not occurred to me in vain. Pompey has gone. He has not found the letter, and--well; that is the end."

But the General had still another theory to account for the delay in the appearance of his mail which he always posed abruptly after the exhaustion of the arraignment of the post-office.

candidates.text:
It was a regular dramatic performance, every first of the month, in the little cottage of the old General and Madame B----.

It began with his wife waking him. She stood at the bedside with a cup of black coffee.

"Hé! Ah! Oh, Honorine! Yes; the first of the month, and affairs—affairs to be transacted."

On the mornings when affairs were to be transacted the household had little leisure, and the household was Honorine. There was no old dressing-gown that day, no slippers, none of the old, old trousers or the antediluvian neck-foulard of other days. Far from it! There was warm water, with a fling of cologne in it. Honorine trimmed his beard and mustache. Then came the black broadcloth suit and the brown satin stock, and that _je ne sais quoi de dégagé_ which no one could possess or assume like the old General. Whether he possessed it or assumed it nobody could say. The same doubt hung over the fine manners of all the gentlemen of his day, who had been kept in Paris through their youth to cultivate _bon ton_ and an education.

It was a gala-day for Madame la Générale too. It must be a gala-day for every old wife to see her husband pranked out in the manners and graces that had conquered her maidenhood. He gave off once more that ambrosial fragrance which had once so well incensed his compelling presence.

Ah, to the end a woman loves to celebrate her conquest! The last misfortune for her is to lose her youthful lord and master in the old, the ugly, and the commonplace. Time thatches old women with gray hairs and wrinkles. But if one could look under them, one would find the flutterings and the quiverings, the thrills, the emotions, the coals of the heart-fires. Only death puts those out, when he commands the tenant to vacate.

Honorine's hands went cold with the ice of sixteen as she brought the scissors to the white mustache and beard. Her finger-tips brushed his lips, still well formed and roseate, and she felt it, strange to say, on her own lips. Then she sprinkled cologne into the warm water. Buying that cologne was her secret delight and her greatest effort of economy. Each time, she had one little moment of what she called faintness. It was the same faintness that had veiled her eyes and chained her hands and stilled her throbbing bosom when she came from the church with him as a bride. That was the day she first noticed the faint fragrance of the cologne bath. Her lips would part as they had parted then. She would stand still a moment and think thoughts she looked forward to, it must be confessed, from one month to the next. He belonged to a period that would take nothing less than physical beauty from Nature, and Nature always gives the period what it asks. If to-day it is all small men, and to-morrow gnomes and dwarfs, we may know the period is demanding them. What a man he had been!

When the General had finished his toilet—let it be called no less than a ceremony—he took his chocolate and his _pain de Paris_. Honorine could not picture him breakfasting on anything but _pain de Paris_. Then he settled into his large arm-chair before the escritoire and began transacting his affairs with the usual—

"But where is that idiot, that dolt, that sluggard, that snail, with my mail?"

Honorine called from the breakfast-room, where she was busy:

"In a moment, husband. In a moment."

"But he should be here now. It is the first of the month, it is nine o'clock, I am ready; he should be here."

"It is not yet nine o'clock, husband."

"Not yet nine! Not yet nine! Am I not up? Am I not dressed? Have I not breakfasted before nine?"

"That is so, husband. That is so." Her voice came promptly and cheerfully from the next room. She was washing his cup, his saucer, and his spoon.

"It is getting worse and worse every day. I tell you, Honorine, Pompey must be discharged. He is worthless. He is trifling. Discharge him! Discharge him! Do not have him about! Chase him out of the yard! Chase him as soon as he makes his appearance! Do you hear, Honorine?"

"You must have a little patience, husband."

Perhaps the only reproach one could make to Madame Honorine was that she never learned by experience.

"Patience! Patience! Patience is the invention of dullards and sluggards. In a well-regulated world there should be no need of such a thing as patience. Patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace. Wherever patience is found police investigation should be made as for smallpox. Patience! Patience! I never heard the word—I assure you, I never heard the word in Paris. What do you think would be said there to the messenger who craved patience of you? Oh, they know too well in Paris—a rataplan from the walking-stick on his back, that would be the answer; and a, 'My good fellow, we are not hiring professors of patience, but legs.'"

"But, husband, you must remember we do not hire Pompey. He only does it to oblige us, out of his kindness."

"Oblige us! Oblige me! Kindness! A negro oblige me! Kind to me! That is it; that is it. That is the way to talk under the new régime. It is favor, and oblige, and education, and monsieur, and madame, now. What child's play to call this a country—a government! I would not be surprised—"

He jumped to his next position. It was the same every first of the month.

"I would not be surprised if Pompey has failed to find the letter in the box. How do I know that the mail has not been tampered with? From day to day I expect to hear it. What is to prevent? Who is to interpose? The honesty of the officials? Honesty of the officials—that is good! What a farce—honesty of officials! That is evidently what has happened. The thought has not occurred to me in vain. Pompey has gone. He has not found the letter, and—well; that is the end."

But the General had one more theory for the lateness of his mail. He always brought it out abruptly, once the arraignment of the post-office was exhausted.

On the first of every month there was a regular dramatic performance in the little cottage of the old General and Madame B----.

It began when his wife woke him. She stood at the bedside with a cup of black coffee.

"Hé! Ah! Oh, Honorine! Yes; the first of the month, and affairs—affairs to be transacted."

On those mornings there was not much leisure for the household, and Honorine was the household. There was no question of the old dressing-gown and slippers, the old, old trousers, the antediluvian neck-foulard of other days. Far from it. There was warm water, with even a fling of cologne in it. Honorine trimmed his beard and mustache. Then came the black broadcloth suit and the brown satin stock, and that _je ne sais quoi de dégagé_ which no one could possess or assume like the old General. Whether he possessed it or assumed it, nobody could say. The same doubt hung over the fine manners of all the gentlemen of his day, who had been kept in Paris through their youth to cultivate _bon ton_ and an education.

It was a gala-day for Madame la Générale too. It must be so for every old wife, to see her husband pranked once more in the manners and graces that had conquered her when she was a girl, and to breathe again the fragrance that had once gone with his commanding presence.

Ah, to the end a woman loves to celebrate her conquest! The last misfortune she can suffer is to lose her youthful lord and master in the old, the ugly, and the commonplace. Time thatches old women with gray hair and wrinkles. But if one could look underneath, one would find the flutterings still there, and the quiverings, the thrills, the emotions, the coals of the heart-fires. Death alone puts those out, when he tells the tenant to vacate.

Honorine's hands went cold as she brought the scissors to the white mustache and beard. It was the ice of sixteen. When her finger-tips brushed his lips, still well formed and rosy, she felt it, strange to say, on her own. She sprinkled the warm water with cologne. Buying it was her secret delight, and it cost her the greatest economy she practised. Each time she had one little moment of what she called faintness. It was the same faintness that had veiled her eyes, and chained her hands, and stilled her throbbing heart when she came from the church with him as a bride. That was the day she had first noticed the faint scent of the cologne bath. Her lips would part as they had parted then. She would stand still a moment and think thoughts which, it must be confessed, she looked forward to from one month to the next.

He had belonged to a period that would take nothing less than physical beauty from Nature, and Nature always gives the period what it asks. If to-day it is all small men, and to-morrow gnomes and dwarfs, it is because the period is demanding them. What a man he had been!

When the General had finished his toilet—it deserved to be called a ceremony—he took his chocolate and his _pain de Paris_. Honorine could not imagine him breakfasting on anything but _pain de Paris_. Then he sat down in his large arm-chair before the escritoire and began to transact his affairs with the usual—

"But where is that idiot, that dolt, that sluggard, that snail, with my mail?"

Honorine was busy in the breakfast-room.

"In a moment, husband. In a moment."

"But he should be here now. It is the first of the month, it is nine o'clock, I am ready; he should be here."

"It is not yet nine o'clock, husband."

"Not yet nine! Not yet nine! Am I not up? Am I not dressed? Have I not breakfasted before nine?"

"That is so, husband. That is so." Her voice came promptly and cheerfully from the next room, where she was washing his cup, saucer, and spoon.

"It is getting worse and worse every day. I tell you, Honorine, Pompey must be discharged. He is worthless. He is trifling. Discharge him! Discharge him! Do not have him about! Chase him out of the yard! Chase him as soon as he shows his face! Do you hear, Honorine?"

"You must have a little patience, husband."

Perhaps the only reproach one could make to Madame Honorine was that she never learned by experience.

"Patience! Patience! Patience is the invention of dullards and sluggards. In a well-regulated world there would be no need of such a thing. Patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace. Wherever patience is found the police should investigate, as for smallpox. Patience! I never heard the word—I assure you, I never heard the word in Paris. What do you think they would say there to a messenger who asked you for patience? Oh, they know too well in Paris. A rataplan from the walking-stick on his back, that would be the answer, and 'My good fellow, we are not hiring professors of patience, but legs.'"

"But, husband, you must remember we do not hire Pompey. He only does it to oblige us, out of kindness."

"Oblige us! Oblige me! Kindness! A negro oblige me! Kind to me! That is it; that is it. That is how they talk under the new régime. It is favor, and oblige, and education, and monsieur, and madame, now. What child's play to call this a country—a government! I would not be surprised"—and here he jumped to the next position of the theme he took up every first of the month—"I would not be surprised if Pompey has not found the letter in the box. How do I know the mail has not been tampered with? I expect to hear it any day. What is to prevent it? Who is to interpose? The honesty of the officials? Honesty of the officials—that is good! What a farce! That is plainly what has happened. The thought did not come to me for nothing. Pompey has gone. He has not found the letter, and—well, that is the end."

But the General had still another theory for the lateness of his mail. He always brought it out abruptly, once he had finished his arraignment of the post-office.

candidates.text:
Every first of the month there was a regular dramatic performance in the little cottage of the old General and Madame B----.

The performance began when the General was woken by his wife. She stood at the bedside with a cup of black coffee.

"Hé! Ah! Oh, Honorine! Yes; the first of the month, and affairs--affairs to be transacted."

On those mornings when affairs were to be transacted there was not much leisure for the household, and the household was Honorine. Not the old dressing-gown and slippers, the old, old trousers, and the antediluvian neck-foulard of other days! Far from it. There was warm water, with even a fling of cologne in it. Honorine trimmed the beard and mustache. Then came the black broadcloth suit and the brown satin stock, and that _je ne sais quoi de dégagé_ which no one could possess or assume like the old General. Whether he possessed it or assumed it, nobody could say. The same uncertainty hung over the fine manners of all the gentlemen of his day, who were kept in Paris through their youth to cultivate _bon ton_ and an education.

Madame la Générale had her gala-day too. Every old wife must have one when she sees her husband pranked once more in the manners and graces that conquered her maidenhood, and breathes again the ambrosial fragrance that once so well incensed his compelling presence. Ah, to the end a woman loves to celebrate her conquest! The last touch of misfortune for her is to lose her youthful lord and master in the old, the ugly, and the commonplace. Time thatches old women with gray hairs and wrinkles. If one could look underneath, one would be surprised to find the flutterings, the quiverings, the thrills, the emotions, the coals of the heart-fires. Death alone puts those out, when he commands the tenant to vacate.

Honorine's hands went cold with the ice of sixteen as she brought the scissors to the white mustache and beard. When her finger-tips brushed his lips, still well formed and roseate, she felt it, strange to say, on her own lips. Then she asperged the warm water with cologne. Buying that cologne was her secret delight and her greatest effort of economy. Each time she had one little moment of what she called faintness. It was the faintness that had veiled her eyes, and chained her hands, and stilled her throbbing bosom, when she came from the church with him as a bride. She had noticed the faint fragrance of the cologne bath for the first time then. Her lips would open as they had opened that day. She would stand for a moment and think thoughts which, it must be confessed, she looked forward to from month to month.

Nature, after all, always gives a period what it asks for. If it is to-day all small men, and to-morrow gnomes and dwarfs, we may know that the period is demanding them from Nature. The General's period would accept nothing less than physical beauty, and what a man he had been!

When the General had completed his toilet (let it be called no less than a ceremony), he took his chocolate and his _pain de Paris_. Honorine could not imagine him breakfasting on anything but _pain de Paris_. Then he sat himself in his large arm-chair before his escritoire, and began transacting his affairs with the usual--

"But where is that idiot, that dolt, that sluggard, that snail, with my mail?"

Honorine was busy in the breakfast-room. "In a moment, husband. In a moment."

"But he should be here now. It is the first of the month, it is nine o'clock, I am ready; he should be here."

"It is not yet nine o'clock, husband."

"Not yet nine! Not yet nine! Am I not up? Am I not dressed? Have I not breakfasted before nine?"

Honorine answered from the next room, prompt in cheerful acquiescence. "That is so, husband. That is so." She was washing his cup, saucer, and spoon.

"It is getting worse and worse every day. I tell you, Honorine, Pompey must be discharged. He is worthless. He is trifling. Discharge him! Discharge him! Do not have him about! Chase him out of the yard! Chase him as soon as he makes his appearance! Do you hear, Honorine?"

"You must have a little patience, husband."

Perhaps the only reproach one could make to Madame Honorine was that she never learned by experience.

"Patience! Patience! Patience is the invention of dullards and sluggards. In a well-regulated world there should be no need of such a thing as patience. Patience should be punished as a crime, or at least as a breach of the peace. Wherever patience is found police investigation should be made as for smallpox. Patience! Patience! I never heard the word--I assure you, I never heard the word in Paris. What do you think would be said there to the messenger who craved patience of you? Oh, they know too well in Paris--a rataplan from the walking-stick on his back, that would be the answer; and a, 'My good fellow, we are not hiring professors of patience, but legs.'"

"But, husband, you must remember we do not hire Pompey. He only does it to oblige us, out of his kindness."

"Oblige us! Oblige me! Kindness! A negro oblige me! Kind to me! Yes, that is it; that is it, the way to talk under the new régime. It is favor, and oblige, and education, and monsieur, and madame, now. What child's play to call this a country--a government! I would not be surprised"--jumping to his next position on this ever-recurring first of the month theme--"I would not be surprised if Pompey has failed to find the letter in the box. How do I know that the mail has not been tampered with? From day to day I expect to hear it. What is to prevent? Who is to interpose? The honesty of the officials? Honesty of the officials--that is good! What a farce--honesty of officials! Evidently the thing has happened. The thought has not occurred to me in vain. Pompey has gone. He has not found the letter, and--well; that is the end."

But the General had still another theory for the lateness of his mail. He always posed it abruptly, once he had exhausted his arraignment of the post-office.
